title: The Man Who Inspired '3 Idiots' Is About to Join India's Gen Z Revolt. He Says He'll Stop Eating Until the Government Listens.
excerpt: Sonam Wangchuk will begin an indefinite hunger strike at Delhi's Jantar Mantar on Sunday, aligning with the Cockroach Janta Party — a meme-born movement that has CNN, the Wall Street Journal, and 20 million Instagram followers paying attention to India's exam crisis.
body:
When Sonam Wangchuk recorded a video outside the United Nations building in Geneva this week, he was standing in front of the Broken Chair monument — a 12-metre wooden sculpture symbolising the struggle for human rights. Behind him was the Palais des Nations. In front of him was a phone camera.

"This is the Jantar Mantar of Geneva," Wangchuk said, referring to Delhi's famous protest site. "Education and environment are my two causes, and I hope at least one of them would be resolved during this week."

It was not resolved. And so the 60-year-old Ladakhi engineer, climate activist, and the real-life inspiration behind Phunsukh Wangdu in the Bollywood hit *3 Idiots* has announced that he will begin an indefinite hunger strike at Jantar Mantar on Sunday, June 28.

## Two Demands, One Deadline

Wangchuk's demands are specific. The first: accountability in the NEET paper leak scandal that has shattered the confidence of millions of students in India's examination system. The second: meaningful action on the constitutional safeguards, statehood, and environmental protections that the people of Ladakh have been demanding since the region was carved out as a Union Territory in 2019.

"If I do not receive a response on either of these issues by Saturday, I will sit on a hunger strike with all of you," Wangchuk said in his video message from Geneva, posted on X on June 25.

Saturday has passed. No response came.

## The Movement He Is Joining

Wangchuk is not arriving at an empty protest site. He is walking into the middle of what may be India's most unusual youth movement in a generation.

The Cockroach Janta Party — a riff on Prime Minister Narendra Modi's ruling Bharatiya Janata Party — was born last month from a remark by India's Chief Justice Surya Kant, whose comments were interpreted as calling the country's unemployed youth "cockroaches." Within days, the party's Instagram account crossed 20 million followers. Its founder, 30-year-old Boston University graduate Abhijeet Dipke, flew from the United States to New Delhi to lead the movement's first street protest.

That first protest at Jantar Mantar on June 6 drew hundreds of students wearing cockroach masks, carrying flowers and tricolours. Wangchuk himself showed up. "I have brought a message of goodwill to everyone," he said that day. "I thank the government for allowing a peaceful protest."

Since then, the CJP has been camped at Jantar Mantar, demanding the resignation of Union Education Minister Dharmendra Pradhan over what protesters describe as a systemic failure to protect India's examination system. The NEET-UG 2026 exam — the gateway for 23 lakh students into medical colleges — was mired in paper leak allegations. The government deployed air force helicopters to transport freshly drafted question papers to over 5,000 test centres for a re-examination, and temporarily blocked the messaging app Telegram over exam fraud channels.

CNN called the CJP "India's viral youth movement." The Wall Street Journal covered the military-grade security around the re-examination. Pradhan dismissed the movement as the "B-team of terrorists." Dipke responded: "Are we asking for votes? We are asking for justice."

## Wangchuk's History of Fasting

This is not Wangchuk's first hunger strike. In March 2024, he fasted for 21 days in sub-zero temperatures in Leh, pressing for Ladakh's inclusion under the Sixth Schedule of the Constitution. In September 2025, he led a 35-day fast alongside 15 supporters. That movement turned violent on September 24, when four people died and 45 were injured in clashes with security forces. The government cancelled the foreign-funding licence of Wangchuk's educational NGO, SECMOL. A CBI probe was launched.

Wangchuk has consistently advocated peaceful protest. "We would rather choose to die staying hungry, taking pain on ourselves, without harming anybody," he said in his September 2025 address.

## Why the Diaspora Should Care

For the Indian diaspora, the convergence of Wangchuk and the CJP touches two raw nerves. The first is the integrity of Indian examinations — a system that produced many of the engineers, doctors, and entrepreneurs now working in the United States, the United Kingdom, Canada, and the Gulf. When NEET leaks, when CUET is compromised, the credential that anchored millions of careers is devalued.

The second is representation. Dipke, a product of the very diaspora pipeline he is now agitating against, gave up a career in the US to fly home and lead a protest. Wangchuk, who has spoken at global forums from Davos to Geneva, is staking his health on the principle that a Union Territory with no legislature, no statehood, and no Sixth Schedule protection is not a democracy — it is an administered silence.

On Sunday morning, if the government has not acted, two of India's most recognisable civic voices — one 60, one 30, one from the Himalayas, one from Boston — will sit together at Jantar Mantar and refuse to eat.

The cockroaches, it turns out, are not going away.
image_caption: Sonam Wangchuk, the Ladakhi engineer and climate activist who inspired the film 3 Idiots
nri_angle: The NEET exam crisis undermines the credentials that propelled millions of diaspora professionals into careers abroad, while the CJP's founder is himself a US-educated Indian who returned to lead the movement.
author: Diaspora Desk
